Question six. What exactly is a p-value? The probability of data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Small means your data would be surprising if nothing were going on. [slowly] Because it assumes the null, it can't be the probability that the null is true, or that your result is a fluke. Question seven. What is hypothesis testing, and what are its steps? State the null and the alternative. Fix the significance level, alpha, and the sample size, before you look. Compute a test statistic and its p-value, and reject the null if p is below alpha. Here, the null is that the two models are equally accurate. Fixing it all in advance is what keeps the test honest. Simulate two equally good models, and check after every two hundred labels: stop at the first p under five percent, and you find a difference nineteen percent of the time, not five.

Question eight. What is a permutation test? It builds the null distribution by shuffling the group labels, which are interchangeable if there's no effect. On the page's two groups of fifty, the difference is five point nine, and ten thousand shuffles match or beat it two point four percent of the time. Now the two models. Pool their four thousand right-or-wrong answers and shuffle, and p is point six two. Nothing there. But they answered the same two thousand examples, and disagree on only eighteen, of which the new model wins fourteen. Shuffle within each pair instead, swapping which model gave which answer, and p is point oh three. Same gap, but the paired test uses how the data was collected, and at five percent it rejects the null.
